item.title: Trump’s Meddling in Justice Dept. Causes Problems of His Own Making
item.description: In the past week alone, President Trump’s interference has imperiled one criminal case, set the stage for sanctions in a second and hindered the confirmation chances of his pick for attorney general.
item.dc:creator: Alan Feuer
item.media:credit: Pete Marovich for The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump has long believed that he enjoys complete control over the agencies beneath him, including the Justice Department.

item.title: Author of Democrats’ 2024 Autopsy Says Party Left Out Key Chapter
item.description: A dispute over the chapter between the author and the Democratic National Committee has added to the party’s turmoil as it tries to look forward, not backward.
item.dc:creator: Shane Goldmacher
item.media:credit: Kent Nishimura for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Democratic National Committee’s autopsy of the 2024 election was meant to examine missteps that led to the party’s defeat.

item.title: Max Miller, Accused of Abuse, Is Not Stepping Aside. Here’s What We Know.
item.description: The Ohio Republican who is seeking a third term defiantly denied domestic abuse allegations ahead of a deadline to replace him on the ballot.
item.dc:creator: Annie Karni
item.media:credit: Eric Lee/The New York Times
item.media:description: Representative Max Miller, Republican of Ohio, and his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, have been in a custody battle that has included abuse allegations since their divorce in 2024.

item.title: After Colleges Reject ‘Compact,’ Trump Officials Try a Letter
item.description: The open letter from Education Secretary Linda McMahon fell far short of the attempt at a compact last year that dangled research money in return for embracing the Trump administration’s agenda.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Bender and Alan Blinder
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: Linda McMahon, the education secretary, signed the letter that asks every postsecondary institution in the nation to publicly state its commitments and planned changes “before the end of 2026.”

item.title: Inside the Secretive Boards Deciding Trans Troops’ Fate
item.description: The Pentagon is relying on closed-door hearings to kick out transgender service members. An Army Reserve lawyer is one of the few who have seen how they really work.
item.dc:creator: Greg Jaffe and Dave Philipps
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Kate Warren for The New York Times
item.media:description: Capt. Kai Proce before his separation board hearing at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in June.

item.title: Here’s Why the US Is Helping Prop Up the Japanese Yen
item.description: The U.S. Treasury joined efforts in Tokyo to stem the yen’s slide against the dollar, highlighting the broader risks posed by turmoil in Japanese markets.

item.title: Spokane Wildfires Destroy Hundreds of Buildings as 60,000 People Evacuate
item.description: Firefighters were hopeful that improving weather conditions in Washington state could help efforts to contain the blaze, which officials described as the largest natural disaster in the history of Spokane.
item.dc:creator: Christina Morales

item.media:description: All of Christine and Bryan Farris’s belongings burned in the Old Trail fire in Spokane, Wash.

item.title: Nanit and Other Baby-Tracking Start-Ups Eye Collecting Even More Data
item.description: Nanit and other start-ups want to track your children through the night — and soon, for much longer than that.
item.dc:creator: Sapna Maheshwari
item.media:credit: Photo illustration by Margeaux Walter for The New York Times
item.media:description: Young parents are increasingly willing to embrace tracking and analytics for their children — part of a broader cultural obsession with health data and optimization.

item.title: For Iran, Trump’s Reversal on Escalation Shows Who Has the Upper Hand

item.title: Kay Granger, Pathbreaking Texas Congresswoman, Dies at 83
item.description: She was the first Republican woman from the state to be elected to the House. It caused a stir in 2024 when she was discovered to be residing in a senior living facility while still in office.
item.dc:creator: Katharine Q. Seelye
item.media:credit: Alyssa Schukar for The New York Times
item.media:description: Representative Kay Granger of Texas at the Capitol in 2023. In her final term, she became the first Republican woman to run the powerful House Appropriations Committee.

item.title: Gen Z Can’t Afford a First Date
item.description: From $130 dinners to expensive cocktails and even exorbitant movie tickets, a crushing economy in New York City is creating a fresh barrier to love.
item.dc:creator: Troy Closson
item.media:credit: Gary Hershorn/Getty Images
item.media:description: People in their 20s and 30s are dating less than earlier generations did. The high cost of going out is one of the reasons.

item.title: Mamdani May Need to Find $5 Billion More a Year for Free Child Care
item.description: A new report by the Center for New York City Affairs projected that a child care system for all children under 5 could cost the city about $9 billion a year.
item.dc:creator: Eliza Shapiro
item.media:credit: Dave Sanders for The New York Times
item.media:description: A new report from the Center for New York City Affairs builds in higher salaries for some New York City child care educators than are included in the current city budget.
